title: Sentinel-1 operational DInSAR services for surface displacements monitoring of the Italian territory through the P-SBAS processing chain: a review after 10 years of observations and data processing
Validation of TROPOMI SIF products based on spatial representativeness grading and atmospheric-geometric effect assessment
abstract: Satellite solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) is important for carbon cycle research, but its direct validation is often hindered by spatial scale mismatch between satellite footprints and in situ measurements. We developed a quantitative spatial representativeness grading framework for in situ SIF measurements. The framework uses two proxy metrics, the consistency index ( 𝐶 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 ) and relative absolute error ( 𝑅 𝐴 ⁢ 𝐸 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 ), to diagnose local SIF simulation consistency and point-to-footprint deviation. Using 6240 HyPlant pseudo-point/footprint samples, a domain-level threshold search yielded Level 1 criteria of 𝐶 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 ∈ [ 0 . 4 , 1 . 0 ] and 𝑅 𝐴 ⁢ 𝐸 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 ≤ 0 . 4 . Samples with the same 𝐶 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 range but 𝑅 𝐴 ⁢ 𝐸 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 > 0 . 4 were classified as Level 2 and required upscaling. We applied this framework to 28 global sites to evaluate three TROPOMI SIF products using Sentinel-2 and ERA5-Land inputs. The framework retained 41–42% of the original matched samples. After controlling spatial scale effects, validation R 2 increased from 0.19 to 0.31 for TROPOSIF 735 and from 0.44 to 0.69 for both TROPOSIF 743 and TROPOSIF Caltech . Sensitivity analyses showed that this improvement was generally preserved under alternative tolerance thresholds and reference confidence criteria, although the proxy thresholds remain empirical. We further assessed cloud and sun-sensor geometry effects. TROPOSIF 735 was sensitive to cloud contamination, whereas TROPOSIF 743 and TROPOSIF Caltech remained robust under moderate cloud cover. Under clear skies, retrieval accuracy declined when solar zenith angle (SZA) exceeded 60 ° , while viewing zenith angle effects were limited after excluding large-SZA observations. Phase angle mismatch introduced systematic bias through canopy SIF anisotropy. Overall, this framework improves direct validation reliability and provides practical guidance for evaluating satellite SIF products.

title: Physics-informed machine learning for cloud detection
abstract: Accurate cloud detection is a critical preprocessing step for analyzing optical remote sensing data, such as from Landsat and Sentinel-2. In this study, we developed Fmask 5 (Version 5 of Function of mask) for cloud detection in Landsats 4–9 (Landsat 4, 5, 7, 8, and 9) and Sentinel-2 (Sentinel-2 A, B, and C) imagery, based on a novel physics-informed machine learning (PIML) framework. This framework synergistically integrates physical rules with machine learning (ML) models, overcoming their respective limitations. Specifically, a base ML model first generates a preliminary cloud mask to adapt to the application of physical rules, determining the optimal combination of spectral tests and thresholds for that image. The resulting physical-rule-adapted mask serves as additional “localized” training data to fine-tune the ML model. For a global, independent validation dataset combining simple random and disagreement-stratified samples from over 600 images per sensor, Fmask 5 achieved overall accuracies of 93.46% for Landsats 8–9, 92.50% for Landsats 4–7, and 95.38% for Sentinel-2, representing improvements of 1.6–6.0 percentage points over Fmask 4. The Fmask 5 algorithm is CPU-efficient, making it suitable for large-scale operational processing.

title: PC2Mesh: Reconstruction of building polygonal meshes from airborne LiDAR point clouds
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Polygonal meshes provide a compact and flexible representation for 3D buildings, supporting a wide range of photogrammetric and geometric applications. However, reconstructing high-fidelity building polygon meshes from airborne LiDAR point clouds remains challenging due to the non-uniform and variable-sided nature of polygonal topology and the complexity of urban environments characterized by diverse building geometries, uneven point densities, and occlusions. In this paper, we present PC2Mesh, a learning-based method that reconstructs polygonal building meshes directly from airborne LiDAR point clouds. While existing approaches rely on primitive detection (e.g., City3D, Point2Poly) or employ separate networks for vertex and face generation (e.g., Point2building), our method employs a unified transformer-based architecture that jointly learns mesh geometry and topology within a shared representation space. By representing arbitrary-sided polygons as learned token sequences, the method enables holistic mesh generation without preprocessing or handcrafted priors. This end-to-end formulation mitigates error propagation across stages and enhances reconstruction fidelity and robustness. Comprehensive experiments on open-source datasets demonstrate that our proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in geometric accuracy and visual fidelity. Our method improves Edge Precision (EP) and Edge Recall (ER) by 9.1% and 24.7%, respectively, on the Zurich dataset, and by 8.3% and 20.2% on the Tallinn dataset. It also achieves the lowest Mean Distance Error (MDE), Hausdorff Distance (HD), and Chamfer Distance (CD) on both datasets. The source code of this work is freely available at https://github.com/BestyHon/PC2Mesh .

title: Topology-preserving river vectorization via HydroSAM and differentiable graph optimization under coarse labels
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Accurate river-network extraction supports global hydrological management and environmental monitoring. Automated extraction from remote-sensing imagery remains challenging because river morphology is highly variable, fine tributaries have weak visual signals, canopy and infrastructure can obscure channels, and dense annotations are scarce or spatially incomplete. Conventional raster predictions can also be fragmented and lack structural continuity. We present HydroSAM, a three-stage framework for raster extraction and topology-aware vectorization. A frozen SAM 2 Hiera encoder is adapted with QV-LoRA and the proposed Directional Curvilinear Prior Injection (DCPI), while a gated Digital Elevation Model (DEM) branch contributes coarse-scale topographic context. Segmentation is produced in a zero-prompt setting by the native SAM 2 mask decoder. A graph-guided differentiable vectorization stage then converts probability maps into connected parametric river networks. We also present M2Hydro, a benchmark containing 7,947 high-resolution 4096 × 4096 source image-annotation pairs across China. In single-run tests, HydroSAM-MM attains an F1 of 0.6995 and clDice of 0.7753 on M2Hydro. The evaluations indicate that HydroSAM supports parameter-efficient adaptation and is more resilient to the evaluated cross-regional domain shift than the convolutional and Transformer baselines.

title: Thinking on maps: how foundation model agents explore, remember, and reason in map environments
abstract: Map environments provide a fundamental medium for representing spatial structure. Understanding how foundation model (FM) agents understand and act in such environments is therefore critical for enabling reliable map-based reasoning and applications. However, most existing evaluations of spatial ability in FMs rely on static map inputs or text-based queries, overlooking the interactive and experience-driven nature of spatial understanding.In this paper, we propose an interactive evaluation framework to analyze how FM agents explore, remember, and reason in symbolic map environments. Agents incrementally explore partially observable grid-based maps consisting of roads, intersections, and points of interest (POIs), receiving only local observations at each step. Spatial understanding is then evaluated using six kinds of spatial tasks. By systematically varying exploration strategies, memory representations, and reasoning schemes across multiple foundation models, we reveal distinct functional roles of these components. Exploration primarily affects experience acquisition but has a limited impact on final reasoning accuracy. In contrast, memory representation plays a central role in consolidating spatial experience, with structured memories particularly sequential and graph-based representations, substantially improving performance on structure-intensive tasks such as path planning. Reasoning schemes further shape how stored spatial knowledge is used, with advanced prompts supporting more effective multi-step inference. We further observe that spatial reasoning performance saturates across model versions and scales beyond a certain capability threshold, indicating that improvements in map-based spatial understanding require mechanisms tailored to spatial representation and reasoning rather than scaling alone.

title: Assessing heat dome effects on forest dynamics in the Pacific Northwest using Planet imagery
abstract: Increasingly frequent extreme heat events are imposing significant stress on forest ecosystems, with implications for both forests and the organisms that depend on them. This study evaluated the effects of the June 2021 Pacific Northwest (PNW) heat dome (a prolonged high-pressure system that generated record-breaking temperatures) on forest canopy health and subsequent recovery within the conifer-dominated Ellsworth Creek Preserve in Washington State, USA, using high-resolution Planet Labs satellite imagery. We analyzed normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) trends from spring through fall from 2017 to 2025 to identify canopy stress and quantify changes in canopy greenness. The experimental forest thinning treatments, designed to accelerate old-growth structural characteristics, allowed us to evaluate canopy responses relative to restoration treatments. Our results showed marked declines in the summer NDVI during and following the 2021 heat dome, indicating substantial canopy stress. These declines differed from patterns observed in preceding years and occurred across all forest treatments. Changes in seasonal NDVI dynamics were evident in the control, thinned, clearcut, and old-growth stands; however, pairwise comparisons showed limited differences among canopy types, indicating broadly similar patterns of NDVI suppression during extreme events. The NDVI trajectories during the four post-heat dome years suggested partial recovery in canopy greenness, although the variability among the treatments remained high and overall NDVI levels remained below Pre2021 conditions in some stands through 2024. The recovery trajectories differed modestly among treatments, but we found limited evidence that canopy density substantially altered either the magnitude of canopy suppression or the subsequent recovery trajectories. Overall, these findings demonstrate that extreme heat events can induce widespread canopy stress across forest types and suggest that canopy structure alone may have a limited influence on canopy-scale responses under extreme atmospheric conditions. These results provide insight for adaptive forest management strategies aimed at maintaining ecosystem function under increasingly extreme climatic conditions.

title: Limited local classification performance but promising spatial transferability of AlphaEarth Foundations for crop mapping across thermal gradients
Evaluating spectral unmixing techniques using imaging spectroscopy data for retrieval of green, non-photosynthetic vegetation, and soil fractional cover
abstract: Estimates of fractional cover of green vegetation (GV), non-photosynthetic vegetation (NPV), and soil provide valuable information about the Earth system. As the new generation of Earth visible-to-shortwave infrared (VSWIR) imaging spectrometers take orbit, global fractional cover data will be obtainable with new and improved spectral unmixing algorithms. Using an ASD Field Spectrometer and the spectral line point intercept (SLPIT) method, we estimate fractional cover from field measurements to compare to contemporaneous airborne (Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer; AVIRIS NG ) and spaceborne (Earth surface Mineral dust source InvesTigation; EMIT) imaging spectroscopy data. Field data were collected in multiple biomes in the US Southwest at 84 validation sites. We used EndMember Combination Monte Carlo (E(MC) 2 ) and Multiple-Endmember Spectral Mixture Analysis (MESMA) to derive fractional cover, two candidate spectral unmixing algorithms used by current (e.g., EMIT) and future imaging spectroscopy missions. Field data exhibited strong agreement between ground and spaceborne/airborne measurements. Our best spectral unmixing approach, E(MC) 2 , produced mean absolute error of ≤0.05 for NPV, GV, and soil with uncertainties ≤0.08 for all classes. We further investigated the performance of global vs. local endmember libraries and found that the global library outperformed the local endmember library. We investigated normalization techniques and their effectiveness with our ground and image fractions. Additionally, we calculated uncertainties from both ground and image fractions. Field results aligned well and within uncertainty predictions from previously reported simulation work. These findings support the use of E(MC) 2 to be used in current and future imaging spectroscopy missions.

title: Elevation-dependent regulation of alpine vegetation productivity by snow cover and grazing on the Tibetan Plateau under a warming–wetting climate
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Grassland productivity on the Tibetan Plateau (TP) is fundamental to regional carbon cycling and ecosystem functioning and is strongly regulated by snow dynamics and grazing under a changing climate. However, the mechanisms by which alpine grassland productivity responds to interacting climatic, cryospheric, and anthropogenic drivers remain poorly constrained. Here, we integrated long-term multi-source Earth observation data to quantify the spatiotemporal trends of grassland gross primary productivity (GPP) across the TP from 1982 to 2018 and examined the relationships between GPP and snow dynamics, climate, and grazing intensity, with an explicit emphasis on elevation-dependent controls. Our results reveal a pronounced nonlinear reorganization of GPP controls along elevation gradients, with a critical transition zone at mid-elevations (∼3500–4000 m). Within this zone, warming exerted the strongest positive association with GPP, while grazing intensity also showed a positive spatial association with GPP. In contrast, at higher elevations (>4500 m), snow dynamics emerged as dominant constraints on GPP. Structural equation modeling further indicates that snow cover duration showed the strongest negative total effect among the modeled environmental variables, whereas grazing intensity showed an elevation – dependent association with GPP, shifting from a positive spatial correlation at mid – elevations to a negative correlation at high elevations. Across all elevation zones, soil moisture-mediated pathways consistently exert stronger controls on GPP than soil temperature pathways, highlighting water availability as the more direct and dominant constraint on alpine grassland productivity. These findings demonstrate that elevation fundamentally regulates the spatial organization of ecosystem productivity controls on the TP and underscore the importance of explicitly accounting for cryosphere–biosphere–human interactions when assessing alpine carbon dynamics under a warming and wetting climate.

title: Active CO2 lidar extends satellite monitoring of urban fossil-fuel CO2 emissions to high-aerosol cities
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Foundation Models
Retrieval of nighttime oceanic liquid cloud optical and microphysical parameters from VIIRS observations: a physics-informed machine learning approach
Piecewise log-normal modeling of Sentinel-1 co-cross polarization coherence and application to wind field Bayesian inversion
abstract: Accurate estimates of kilometer-scale ocean surface wind fields is critical for many applications, including weather forecasting, marine navigation, offshore wind energy development, and coastal risk management. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) plays a key role in retrieving wind speed by analyzing changes in sea surface roughness, described through Geophysical Model Functions (GMFs). However, the inverse problem of wind retrieval from SAR data is under-determined, requiring ancillary information from Numerical Weather Models (NWP) to resolve ambiguities in the wind direction. The Co-Cross-Polarization Coherence (CCPC) has recently emerged as a valuable SAR-derived observation for improving wind direction estimates. While an initial GMF for CCPC has been proposed, it proved inadequate for high wind speeds. We present PGMF-2, a refined GMF for CCPC, ensuring reliable performance up to approximately 25 m/s by modeling its wind speed components as log-normal functions. The need for crosstalk calibration is mitigated by a burst-based processing. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that the unique odd-symmetry of the CCPC and the different impact of the wind direction modulation on its real and imaginary parts complements the Normalized Radar Cross Section (NRCS) to estimate the wind direction. This combination enables wind direction retrieval without NWP priors, even outperforming NWP-based inversions between 7 and 15 m/s. The Mean Absolute Error on direction reaches as low as 25 ∘ in favorable (in particular between 30 ∘ –90 ∘ and 270 ∘ –330 ∘ of wind direction relative to the satellite antenna, where the NRCS and the CCPC have overlapping wind direction variability) high-wind conditions. Co-observations with the HY-2B scatterometer, supplemented by a case study on Storm Alex (2020), serve as a proof of concept of the Bayesian scheme on real-world observations, successfully retrieving the typical flow organization of the cyclonic system without reliance on NWP priors.

title: Remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments: A critical review and integrated analysis of Lastarria volcano
abstract: Hydrothermal alteration is a key process in active volcanic systems, influencing edifice stability, fluid circulation, degassing pathways, and volcanic hazards. Remote sensing is widely used to map hydrothermal alteration; however, many approaches treat alteration-related surfaces as static targets, so their reliability, transferability, and process significance in active volcanic environments remain insufficiently evaluated. This study synthesizes commonly used remote sensing approaches and examines the behavior and interpretive implications of representative outputs at Lastarria volcano, which is an arid, high-altitude, vegetation-free system with active fumarolic fields. We compare visual interpretation, VNIR-SWIR reflectance products, pixel-based and sub-pixel mapping outputs, UAV thermal infrared observations, and LiDAR-derived surface-state information. The results show that visual interpretation, reflectance-based products, and pixel-based or sub-pixel outputs delineate broad alteration-related patterns, but their extent, internal structure, and interpretive meaning vary with methodological choices, surface mixing, and environmental surface states. Thermal infrared observations constrain apparent surface-temperature anomalies and fumarole-proximal activity, whereas LiDAR-derived products provide complementary information on surface state, morphology, and roughness. These observations do not converge on a single alteration representation; instead, they capture different aspects of the volcanic-hydrothermal system. Environmental, climatic, and surface controls, including exposure state, moisture, surface reworking, and seasonality, further limit direct transferability among volcanic settings. We suggest that remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments should move from deterministic mapping toward process-oriented and uncertainty-aware interpretation, with temporal persistence, spatial coherence, process plausibility, and independent support providing a basis for future multi-temporal analysis and monitoring.

title: DescribeEarth: Detailed localized captioning for remote sensing images
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Automated textual description of remote sensing images is crucial for unlocking their full potential in diverse applications, from environmental monitoring to urban planning and disaster management. However, existing studies in remote sensing image captioning primarily focus on the image level, lacking object-level fine-grained interpretation, which prevents the full utilization and transformation of the rich semantic and structural information contained in remote sensing images. Consequently, we propose Geo-DLC, a novel task for fine-grained object-level image captioning in remote sensing. To systematically establish and evaluate this new paradigm, we introduce a comprehensive suite encompassing a dataset, a benchmark, and a specialized model. Specifically, we construct DE-Dataset, a large-scale collection comprising 25 categories and 261,806 annotated instances with detailed descriptions of object attributes, relationships, and contexts. To provide a rigorous evaluation standard, we develop DE-Benchmark, an LLM-assisted evaluation protocol based on question answering, to accurately measure the capabilities of models on the Geo-DLC task. Furthermore, we present DescribeEarth, an MLLM architecture explicitly tailored for this task. It integrates a scale-adaptive focal strategy and a domain-guided fusion module, which leverage the features of remote sensing Vision-Language Model (VLM) to encode high-resolution details and category priors while maintaining the global context. Extensive evaluations show that DescribeEarth achieves the highest aggregate scores on the simple and complex subsets and matches GPT-4o on the out-of-distribution subset of DE-Benchmark. Its clearest gains occur in surrounding-context coverage and in categories whose interpretation depends strongly on overhead spatial layout and remote-sensing context. All data, code, and weights are publicly available at https://github.com/earth-insights/DescribeEarth .

title: 160 Years of Etna summit craters through a photogrammetry-based time machine
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: This study presents a quantitative, multi-temporal assessment of Etna’s summit morpho-structural evolution, spanning a 160-year (1865–2024) period. We integrated historical topographic maps with modern, high-resolution remote sensing data, including Unoccupied Aerial System surveys. Dataset-specific validation and statistical error propagation yielded root mean square errors ranging from decametric values for the earliest cartographic sources to metric values for the post-2020 datasets. The resulting topographic time series was interpreted alongside geological observations and previously published geodetic analyses. This integrated reconstruction documents the transition from a predominantly monocentric summit configuration to a highly dynamic polycentric system, and reveals contrasting morpho-structural behaviours among the four summit craters. VOR is characterized by recent constructive growth, BN and NEC by recurrent infilling followed by subsidence, whereas the SEC exhibits persistent constructive growth accompanied by progressive eastward expansion. These differences are consistent with variations in crater position, structural setting, shallow feeding-system configuration, and dominant eruptive style. The long-term evolution of the summit area is also consistent with the influence of the North-East and South Rift zones, and with published geodetic observations describing the seaward deformation of Etna’s eastern flank. Overall, the reconstructed evolution highlights the interaction between volcanic construction, structural controls, and gravitational deformation in shaping a continuously changing and asymmetric summit system. The proposed geospatial workflow provides a reproducible and transferable framework for integrating heterogeneous historical and modern topographic datasets and for investigating long-term morpho-structural change at other highly active volcanoes.

title: Atmospheric restoration is a prerequisite for sub-pixel fire mapping: A smoke-robust protocol across five fire regions
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Wildfires exert profound impacts on global ecosystems; however, accurate satellite-based burn area extraction is frequently confounded by the inherent mixed-pixel issue and complex atmospheric conditions. Although sub-pixel mapping (SPM) can resolve the mixed pixel issue, the extent to which its extraction accuracy depends on initial atmospheric preprocessing under diverse haze and smoke conditions remains poorly quantified. Furthermore, the conditions under which such preprocessing remains effective, and the boundary of its operational envelope, are not well understood. This study introduces a Smoke-Robust Sub-pixel Mapping (SRSPM) protocol to systematically diagnose atmospheric preprocessing efficacy prior to SPM. Using both simulated and real atmospheric states across five distinct fire regions, we systematically evaluate the sensitivity of sub-pixel fire perimeter delineation to different levels of haze contamination. Our findings demonstrate that atmospheric scattering inherently degrades the spatial allocation capabilities of SPM, leading to severe omission errors. Restoring contaminated spectral signals is shown to be essential, rather than merely beneficial, for accurate mapping when haze contamination is substantial. Crucially, our quantitative diagnosis reveals the operational limits of the SRSPM protocol: the dehazing benefit grows with haze intensity and remains substantial up to the strongest simulated contamination ( w = 1); in one region it turns positive only beyond w ≈0.73, delineating the quantitative envelope of the SRSPM protocol. Overall, this work establishes the SRSPM protocol as a practical diagnostic tool for quantifying the interaction between atmospheric correction and sub-pixel spatial allocation, providing empirical guidance for operational disaster monitoring in complex atmospheric environments.

title: Improving automatic glacier mapping accuracy, robustness, and reliability across the Third Pole Region
abstract: Most automatic glacier mapping methods applied in the Third Pole Region (TPR), exhibit suboptimal accuracy for debris-covered glaciers, high sensitivity to interferences, and large uncertainty in model outputs, thereby limiting their operational utility. These challenges can be mitigated by deploying advanced deep learning models and enhancing dataset representativeness across complex imaging conditions. Accordingly, we compiled three large-scale datasets used for model development, glacier-level mapping evaluation, and cross-sensor generalisation assessment, respectively. We then evaluated several state-of-the-art deep learning networks and found that the adapted TransUNet performed best. On the test dataset, the model achieves a glacier Intersection over Union (IoU) of 90% and 83% in patches featuring debris-free and debris-covered glaciers, respectively, while maintaining robust under challenging conditions. Glacier-level validation further confirms the effective detection of glacier counts and precise outlines, with both metrics improving with glacier area and the global IoUTPR > 80%. Uncertainty quantification shows high output reliability, with expected calibration errors of 0.029 and 0.009 for the test and glacier-level test datasets, respectively. Our fully automated 2024–2025 Karakoram glacier inventory, comprising 12,981 glaciers covering a total area of ~19,484 km2, exhibits high agreement with earlier inventories and reflects current glacier state. The primary contribution of this study is the development of a scalable framework that, by optimising dataset representativeness and algorithmic architectures, significantly elevates the accuracy, robustness, reliability and operational value of glacier mapping across the TPR.

title: Fusing SAR and SWIM observations to improve the global stokes drift estimates
A multi-sensor and multi-temporal GeoAI framework for resolving ecological scale mismatch in Antarctica
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Advances in remote sensing (RS) and artificial intelligence (AI) are enabling new approaches to ecological monitoring across spatial and temporal scales. However, vegetation mapping in polar environments remains constrained by a fundamental mismatch between the fine spatial scale of ecological processes and the coarse resolution of satellite observations, as well as by limited availability of biologically reliable training data. In this study, we address these challenges by developing an end-to-end GeoAI framework that integrates field observations, drone imagery, and satellite time-series data to enable cross-scale vegetation mapping. We propose a progressive weak-to-strong labelling workflow that begins with 1) biologically grounded quadrat annotations, to create iteratively expanded training data along with 2) spectral similarity combined with machine learning, followed by 3) training with deep learning (DL) models for pixel-level segmentation. Native Sentinel-2 observations (10–20 m spatial resolution) were processed using DL-based super-resolution to an approximately 1 m output grid. High-resolution drone DL predictions were subsequently transformed into fractional cover labels aligned to the super-resolved satellite grid, supporting cross-scale modelling across centimetre-to-metre resolutions. We evaluate multiple DL architectures using spatially separated UAV evaluation data and assess satellite-scale performance as agreement with UAV-derived fractional cover reference labels. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially improves the scalability and ecological relevance of vegetation mapping in data-limited environments. The best-performing drone-scale DL model (DeepLabv3+) achieved an overall accuracy of 0.91 and a Macro-F1 score of 0.85 for fine-scale vegetation segmentation. At the satellite scale, the U-Net fractional-cover model achieved strong predictive performance for dominant vegetation classes, including cyanobacteria (R 2 = 0.94) and red Hennediella heimii moss (R 2 = 0.88), with reduced performance for spectrally complex or sparsely represented classes, demonstrating effective cross-scale vegetation mapping despite challenges associated with sub-pixel heterogeneity and spectral mixing. This study provides a generalisable methodological framework for integrating multi-sensor data and AI in ecological RS, demonstrating strong cross-scale performance while illustrating the challenges of capturing fine-scale vegetation heterogeneity at satellite scales.

title: Bridging cloud-induced gaps in MODIS leaf area index products using high-frequency geostationary satellite observations
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Leaf Area Index (LAI) is a fundamental variable for characterizing vegetation canopy structure and ecosystem functioning. However, persistent cloud contamination substantially constrains the spatiotemporal continuity of LAI products derived from polar-orbiting satellite observations. In contrast, geostationary satellites provide dense temporal sampling, offering a valuable observational basis for filling data gaps in polar-orbiting satellite products. To bridge this observational gap, this study develops an observation-complementary framework that integrates high-frequency Himawari-8 Advanced Himawari Imager (AHI) observations with MODIS LAI products to achieve LAI reconstruction in cloud-prone regions. Within this framework, AHI observations are first used to retrieve LAI at a spatial resolution of 2 km using a Random Forest model trained with a high-quality MODIS-based benchmark dataset, and are then downscaled to 500 m using MODIS-derived spatial texture information. The reconstructed AHI LAI is subsequently integrated into low-quality or missing MODIS pixels to generate a fused AHI-MODIS LAI dataset over China. Validation against in-situ measurements and cross-comparison results show that the fused product maintains reasonable numerical consistency and stable temporal trajectories. Data availability increases from 70.70% to 90.90% under the 4-day compositing cycle. These results indicate that geostationary-polar-orbiting observation complementarity provides a practical pathway for improving the continuity and usability of optical LAI products in persistently cloudy regions, while remaining subject to the constraints of optical observations and cross-scale reconstruction assumptions.

title: BD-Diff: Generative Diffusion Model for Image Deblurring on Unknown Domains with Blur-Decoupled Learning
TAME-MA: Taming Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Level Trustworthiness Under Jailbreak Manipulations
PosePAL: Efficient Animal Pose Labeling Using Point Trackers
abstract: Abstract Automatically estimating animal poses from videos is important for studying animal behavior. Existing methods do not perform reliably, partly because they rely on high-quality training data, and existing such datasets are small. It is challenging and expensive to create such data, due to the large variations in animal morphology and the difficulty of frame-wise video annotation in general. In this paper, we introduce an animal pose labeling pipeline that leverages test-time optimization of a point tracker, providing temporally-consistent annotations at low cost. Given a video, we fine-tune a lightweight appearance embedding inside a pre-trained general-purpose point tracker on a sparse set of annotated frames. These annotations can be obtained from human labelers or off-the-shelf pose detectors. The fine-tuned model is then applied to the rest of the frames for automatic labeling. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance at a reasonable annotation cost. We believe our pipeline offers a valuable tool for the automatic quantification of animal behavior. Visit our project webpage at https://zhuoyang-pan.github.io/animal-labeling .

title: Voxelized 3D Gaussian Representation for Dense Visual SLAM on Embedded Vision System
Pseudo-label Refinement and Model-State Recovery for Continual Test-Time Adaptation on Semantic Segmentation
Sampling-Free Universal Domain Adaptive Object Detection with Synergistic Optimization Alignment
abstract: Abstract Universal Domain Adaptive Object Detection (UniDAOD) addresses domain shifts in open-world scenarios without assuming pre-defined shared categories between source and target domains. Despite progress in this field, existing methods rely heavily on thresholding techniques to filter private category samples, which introduces challenges in hyperparameter tuning and handling noisy data. To overcome these limitations, we propose Synergistic Optimization Alignment (SOA), a sampling-free framework that tackles two challenges inherent in UniDAOD: multi-scale discriminator discrepancy and task-dominant gradient conflict. To address the discrepancy among multi-scale discriminators, we propose Multi-Scale Discriminator Alignment (MDA) to adaptively aggregate under-aligned discriminators for shared classes, ensuring consistent feature alignment across scales. To address task-dominant gradient conflicts, we propose Gradient Coordinated Optimization (GCO), which suppresses conflicting domain-alignment gradients and coordinates their magnitudes to prevent domain over-alignment, thereby mitigating private-class interference while preserving beneficial domain-invariant supervision. Extensive experiments on open-set, partial-set, and closed-set domain adaptation benchmarks demonstrate that SOA outperforms state-of-the-art UniDAOD and DAOD methods. Code is available at https://github.com/zyfone/SOA .

title: TeD-Loc: Text distillation for weakly supervised object localization
abstract: Weakly supervised object localization (WSOL) models are trained using only image-level class labels. They can predict both the object class and spatial regions corresponding to the object, without requiring explicit bounding box annotations. Given their reliance on classification objectives, traditional WSOL methods, like class activation mapping, tend to focus on the most discriminative object regions, often missing the full spatial extent. Although vision-language models such as CLIP encode rich semantic priors, they are not directly suited for WSOL because global text and class-token embeddings are not explicitly aligned with local patch embeddings, making patch-level localization difficult without additional mechanisms. Recent methods such as GenPrompt address this limitation, but at the cost of increased complexity, as they rely on conditional denoising and elaborate prompt-learning strategies. We propose Text Distillation for Localization (TeD-Loc), which transfers knowledge from CLIP text embeddings to patch embeddings through contrastive alignment, thereby enabling patch-level foreground/background localization. A localization-guided classification module is also introduced that uses localization scores to aggregate foreground patch embeddings for joint classification and localization in a single model. In addition, a QR-based orthogonalization of class text embeddings is applied before distillation to improve discrimination for semantically similar classes. Extensive experiments show that TeD-Loc improves Top-1 Loc by ~5% on CUB and ILSVRC, and PxAP by ~31% on histopathology benchmarks, while achieving more efficient inference than GenPrompt.

title: Multi-level Synergy Alignment Framework for weakly supervised visible-infrared person re-identification
abstract: Visible-infrared person re-identification (VI-ReID) is an important task for all-weather surveillance, but it remains challenging due to significant modality discrepancies and the high cost of annotating cross-modality identity correspondences. To reduce annotation dependence, this paper focuses on weakly supervised VI-ReID, where only intra-modality identity labels are available and explicit cross-modality identity correspondences are absent. We propose a Multi-level Synergy Alignment Framework (MSAF) to improve cross-modality representation learning from the signal representation, structural semantics, and optimization reliability level. In MSAF, the Cross-Spectral Consensus Block (CSCB) performs frequency-domain decomposition and adaptive fusion to integrate complementary low- and high-frequency cues and enhance cross-spectral structural representations. The Self-Organized Semantic Anchoring (SOSA) module discovers discriminative local semantic anchors with learnable prototypes and constructs a global-local pedestrian representation. The Uncertainty-Driven Expert Synergy (UDES) mechanism estimates sample-level reliability and modulates cross-modality prediction scores to reduce the influence of noisy pseudo labels. Extensive experiments on the SYSU-MM01 and LLCM datasets demonstrate that MSAF achieves superior performance among weakly supervised methods.

title: ST-SpikFormer: Spike-driven Transformer using Spatio-Temporal Fusion coding
Mapping rodent-induced disturbance of biological soil crusts using PlanetScope imagery and deep-learning-informed graph cut
abstract: Biological soil crusts (biocrusts) function as a “living skin” at the soil–atmosphere interface and provide important ecosystem services in drylands. While climate change and anthropogenic disturbances are well-recognized drivers of biocrust degradation, mechanical disturbance by wildlife remains poorly understood. Burrowing rodents can directly damage biocrusts by excavating and displacing soil, creating bright disturbance patches that contrast sharply with the darker surrounding biocrust matrix. Based on this brightness contrast, we developed a mapping framework using high-resolution PlanetScope basemaps from 2017 to 2025 to delineate rodent-induced biocrust disturbance in the Gurbantunggut Desert, China. The framework follows a two-stage strategy. First, a Swin-UPerNet model generates colony probability maps to capture diverse colony patterns. Second, these maps are refined using a morphology-based scoring scheme to enhance small and weakly expressed patches, and then optimized by graph cut using brightness-gradient information to sharpen boundaries. Validation against 125 independent field-supported reference sites showed that the framework achieved an overall accuracy (OA) of 97.52% (97.10–97.92%), with an F1-score of 0.804 (0.778–0.826) and an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.672 (0.636–0.703) for the disturbance class. Rodent-induced disturbance was spatially extensive, reaching 1218.34 km 2 (1157.87–1284.25 km 2 ) in 2019 and comprising approximately 1.11 million mapped disturbance patches. This mapped footprint was equivalent to 10.3% of the estimated fractional biocrust-cover area for that year, indicating that rodent excavation occupied a substantial area that could otherwise support biocrust cover. The extent of mapped disturbance was highly dynamic over time, declining sharply through 2022, reaching a minimum in 2023, and then rebounding rapidly through 2025. Representative trajectories further suggest that rodent-induced disturbance can expand rapidly and persist for years, and that its dynamics may be coupled with hydroclimatic stress in biocrust-covered landscapes. These findings highlight rodent-induced disturbance as an important yet underrecognized component of desert ecosystem dynamics and provide a remote-sensing framework for monitoring such disturbances under a changing climate.

title: HELIOS-Net: Hourly daytime estimation of land surface temperature with integration of observational solar-cloud-satellite geometry and deep neural network
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Geostationary satellite-based land surface temperature (LST) is vital for monitoring diurnal thermal dynamics owing to its extensive spatial coverage and high temporal resolution. However, frequent cloud cover results in substantial data gaps, limiting its practical utility for reliable thermal monitoring applications. The solar-cloud-satellite geometry (SCSG) effect has recently been introduced to reflect direct cloud radiative effects in LST reconstruction, but its application has been largely limited to polar-orbiting satellites. To address this limitation, we propose HELIOS-Net, a deep learning (DL) framework for hourly daytime LST reconstruction using the GEO-KOMPSAT-2A satellite across South Korea, central Japan, and southeastern Australia. The framework combines SCSG-based regime partitioning with a generative adversarial network (GAN) to reconstruct spatially continuous all-sky LST by leveraging satellite observations and various meteorological and topographic variables. Validation against in-situ observations demonstrated that HELIOS-Net achieved high performance across all regions, with coefficient of determination (R 2 ) values of 0.63–0.94 and root mean square error (RMSE) values of 2.45–7.65 °C under cloudy-sky conditions. Comparative evaluation further indicated an overall performance advantage over ERA5-Land and an existing all-sky LST product derived from satellite observations. Additional analyses confirmed that both the SCSG effect and the DL framework contribute to enhancing the fidelity of hourly daytime LST reconstruction. These results highlight the potential of the proposed framework to enable high-quality, spatially continuous all-sky LST monitoring from geostationary satellites, providing a promising approach mitigating cloud-induced data gaps under diverse viewing geometries and environmental conditions.

title: SNAIL-Radar-Indoor:A large-scale handheld LiDAR–4D radar–IMU dataset for robust SLAM in degraded environments
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Multimodal sensing, particularly 4D imaging radar, is promising for emergency search and rescue because it remains informative under smoke and highly reflective structures. However, existing public radar datasets predominantly record outdoor vehicle motion or clean indoor spaces. We present SNAIL-Radar-Indoor, a large-scale handheld LiDAR–4D radar–IMU dataset for SLAM in smoke and other degraded environments. Extending our previous outdoor SNAIL-Radar benchmark, the new release contains 217 sequences totaling approximately 850 min, collected at 13 sites across six scene types, including offices, abandoned buildings, halls, factory workshops, underground parking areas, and connecting outdoor spaces. The sequences cover corridors, rooms, staircases, narrow corners, indoor–outdoor transitions, reflective structures, dynamic crowds, and real smoke. Data were recorded using a compact self-developed integrated platform comprising a 3D LiDAR, a low-cost single-chip 4D imaging radar, a consumer-grade IMU, and an optional barometer. Repeated traversals and closed paths are included where feasible to support place recognition and loop-closure evaluation. The released trajectories are method-generated references and do not constitute independent absolute ground truth. Smoke-free sequences mainly use loop-consistent LIO references; fully smoke-dominated sequences use an iRIOM-based radar–IMU reference with AHRS and barometer constraints; and partially degraded sequences use a smoke-aware piecewise RLIO reference. Closed sequences additionally include start–end LiDAR registration constraints, while non-closed sequences are accompanied by map-based end-to-end displacement checks. The dataset supports research on radar and multimodal registration, smoke-robust odometry and mapping, denoising, environmental perception, and navigation in degraded environments.

title: SaKD: Lightweight infrared small target detection via Spatial-Aware Knowledge Distillation for edge deployment
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurate infrared small target detection (IRSTD) in remote sensing remains challenging because targets of interest typically occupy only a few pixels and provide limited spatial cues against complex backgrounds. Existing high-performance methods rely on complex networks to enhance weak target representations, limiting their use on resource-constrained edge devices. Lightweight models reduce computation but struggle to capture scarce spatial cues of small targets. To preserve these spatial cues in lightweight models for remote sensing applications, we propose SaKD, a Spatial-Aware Knowledge Distillation method for IRSTD. SaKD explicitly captures complementary spatial cues associated with target responses from teacher predictions, thereby providing richer spatial discriminative supervision for the student model. Without changing the student inference structure, SaKD introduces two training stage components. The Multi-Scale Self Guidance Mechanism first derives auxiliary supervision from the student’s own responses at multiple scales to strengthen target representation before teacher guidance is introduced. Spatial Prior Distillation then transfers the teacher’s spatial priors by enforcing region, position, and scale consistency, corresponding to target region coverage, center localization, and response scale control. Experiments on multiple IRSTD datasets containing real remote sensing imagery show that SaKD consistently improves the undistilled lightweight student and achieves competitive detection performance with low model complexity. The distilled student contains only 0.895M parameters and 1.999G FLOPs. Deployment verification on a Jetson platform further demonstrates its practical efficiency for edge deployable remote sensing applications, reaching 142.7 FPS for standalone TensorRT FP16 inference at an input resolution of 256 × 256. The code will be available at: https://github.com/Kingwin97/SaKD .
